cards.q: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons.
cards.a:
Oxidation is the loss of electrons.
Reduction is the gain of electrons.
cards.why: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain. The two always happen together, so the reaction is called redox.

cards.q: Define an oxidising agent and a reducing agent.
cards.a:
An oxidising agent is an electron acceptor: it gains electrons and is itself reduced.
A reducing agent is an electron donor: it loses electrons and is itself oxidised.
cards.why: The oxidising agent takes electrons from the species it oxidises.

cards.q: True or false: an oxidising agent is oxidised in a reaction.
cards.a: False. An oxidising agent is reduced: it gains the electrons lost by the species it oxidises.
cards.why: In \(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2Br^{-} \rightarrow 2Cl^{-} + Br_{2}}\), chlorine is the oxidising agent and is reduced to chloride ions.

cards.q: In general, how do metals and non-metals form ions, and what happens to their oxidation numbers?
cards.a:
Metals lose electrons to form positive ions: their oxidation number increases (oxidation).
Non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions: their oxidation number decreases (reduction).
cards.why: \(\mathrm{Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^{-}}\) (0 to +2); \(\mathrm{O_{2} + 4e^{-} \rightarrow 2O^{2-}}\) (0 to −2).

cards.q: What is meant by the oxidation number (oxidation state) of an element in a compound or ion?
cards.a: The charge an atom of the element would have if all its bonds were fully ionic, with the electrons in each bond given to the more electronegative atom.
cards.why: It is a bookkeeping number: an increase means oxidation, a decrease means reduction.

cards.q: State the basic rules for assigning oxidation numbers.
cards.a:
Uncombined element: 0.
Simple ion: its charge.
The oxidation numbers in a neutral compound add up to 0; in an ion they add up to its charge.
Usual values: F −1; O −2; H +1; Group 1 +1; Group 2 +2; Cl −1 (except with O or F).
cards.why: Apply the fixed values first, then work out the unknown element so the total is right.

cards.q: Give the exceptions to the usual oxidation numbers of oxygen and hydrogen.
cards.a:
Oxygen is −1 in peroxides (\(\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}\), \(\mathrm{Na_{2}O_{2}}\)) and +2 in \(\mathrm{OF_{2}}\).
Hydrogen is −1 in metal hydrides (\(\mathrm{NaH}\), \(\mathrm{CaH_{2}}\)).
cards.why: Fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen, and a metal is less electronegative than hydrogen.

cards.q: Find the oxidation number of sulfur in \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\).
cards.a: +6
cards.why: A neutral compound: the oxidation numbers add up to zero.

cards.q: Find the oxidation number of manganese in \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\).
cards.a: +7
cards.why: In an ion the oxidation numbers add up to the charge on the ion.

cards.q: Find the oxidation number of chromium in \(\mathrm{Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}}\).
cards.a: +6
cards.why: Divide by the number of chromium atoms at the end.

cards.q: Find the oxidation number of nitrogen in \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\) and in \(\mathrm{NO_{3}^{-}}\).
cards.a: −3 in \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\); +5 in \(\mathrm{NO_{3}^{-}}\)
cards.why: The same element can have very different oxidation numbers in different species.

cards.q: Find the oxidation number of oxygen in \(\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}\) and of hydrogen in \(\mathrm{NaH}\).
cards.a: −1 for O in \(\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}\); −1 for H in \(\mathrm{NaH}\)
steps: \(\mathrm{NaH}\): Na is always +1, so \(+1 + x = 0\) and \(x = -1\)
cards.why: Peroxides and metal hydrides are the standard exceptions to O = −2 and H = +1.

cards.q: Find the oxidation number of sulfur in the thiosulfate ion, \(\mathrm{S_{2}O_{3}^{2-}}\), and in the tetrathionate ion, \(\mathrm{S_{4}O_{6}^{2-}}\).
cards.a: +2 in \(\mathrm{S_{2}O_{3}^{2-}}\); +2.5 in \(\mathrm{S_{4}O_{6}^{2-}}\)
cards.why: A fractional value is an average over atoms that are not all in the same environment; it is still useful for counting electrons.

cards.q: Find the oxidation number of carbon in the ethanedioate ion, \(\mathrm{C_{2}O_{4}^{2-}}\), and of vanadium in \(\mathrm{VO_{2}^{+}}\).
cards.a: +3 for C; +5 for V
cards.why: When ethanedioate is oxidised to \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\), carbon goes from +3 to +4.

cards.q: How is the oxidation number of iron in \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) written, and how does that differ from the charge on the ion?
cards.a: Oxidation number: +2 (sign first). Ion charge: 2+ (number first), as in \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\).
cards.why: Writing the oxidation number as “2+” loses marks; oxidation numbers always carry a sign, even +1 and −1.

cards.q: What does the Roman numeral in a name such as iron(III) chloride or potassium manganate(VII) show?
cards.a: The oxidation number of the element it follows: iron is +3 in iron(III) chloride; manganese is +7 in potassium manganate(VII).
cards.why: It is needed when an element can have more than one oxidation number.

cards.q: Name these ions using Roman numerals: \(\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}\), \(\mathrm{SO_{3}^{2-}}\), \(\mathrm{ClO^{-}}\), \(\mathrm{ClO_{3}^{-}}\), \(\mathrm{NO_{2}^{-}}\).
cards.a: Sulfate(VI), sulfate(IV), chlorate(I), chlorate(V), nitrate(III).
cards.why: The numeral is the oxidation number of the central atom: Cl is +1 in \(\mathrm{ClO^{-}}\) and +5 in \(\mathrm{ClO_{3}^{-}}\).

cards.q: Write formulae for: copper(I) oxide; iron(II) hydroxide; sodium chlorate(V); iron(III) sulfate.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Cu_{2}O}\); \(\mathrm{Fe(OH)_{2}}\); \(\mathrm{NaClO_{3}}\); \(\mathrm{Fe_{2}(SO_{4})_{3}}\)
cards.why: Balance the charges: two \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\) for one \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\); two \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) for three \(\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}\); Cl at +5 needs three O for a 1− ion.

cards.q: How can oxidation numbers be used to decide whether a reaction is a redox reaction?
cards.a: Work out the oxidation number of each element before and after. If any element’s oxidation number changes, it is a redox reaction: an increase is oxidation and a decrease is reduction.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3} + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_{2} + H_{2}O + CO_{2}}\) is not redox: no oxidation number changes.

cards.q: In \(\mathrm{2Fe^{2+}(aq) + Cl_{2}(aq) \rightarrow 2Fe^{3+}(aq) + 2Cl^{-}(aq)}\), what is oxidised, what is reduced, and which is the oxidising agent?
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is oxidised (+2 to +3); chlorine is reduced (0 to −1). \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\) is the oxidising agent.
steps: The species reduced, \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\), is the oxidising agent; \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is the reducing agent.
cards.why: Two Fe each lose one electron; one Cl₂ gains two. Electrons lost equal electrons gained.

cards.q: Use oxidation numbers to show that \(\mathrm{2Na(s) + Cl_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2NaCl(s)}\) is a redox reaction.
cards.a: Sodium is oxidised (0 to +1) and chlorine is reduced (0 to −1).
steps: Na: 0 in the element, +1 in \(\mathrm{NaCl}\): increase, oxidised.
cards.why: Forming an ionic compound from its elements is always redox.

cards.q: When sodium burns in chlorine, sodium is described as the reducing agent. Explain why, in terms of electrons and oxidation numbers.
cards.a: Sodium gives electrons to chlorine, reducing it.
marks: Each sodium atom loses one electron: \(\mathrm{Na \rightarrow Na^{+} + e^{-}}\).
Its oxidation number increases from 0 to +1, so sodium is oxidised.
Chlorine gains the electrons (\(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow 2Cl^{-}}\)), so its oxidation number falls from 0 to −1.
Sodium is an electron donor, which is what a reducing agent is.

cards.q: What is a disproportionation reaction?
cards.a: A redox reaction in which the same element in a single species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.
cards.why: Oxidation numbers show it: one element in one reactant goes both up and down.

cards.q: Show that the reaction of chlorine with cold dilute sodium hydroxide is a disproportionation: \(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2NaOH \rightarrow NaCl + NaClO + H_{2}O}\).
cards.a: Chlorine goes from 0 to −1 (reduced) and from 0 to +1 (oxidised).
steps: Cl in \(\mathrm{NaCl}\): −1, a decrease, so reduced.
Cl in \(\mathrm{NaClO}\): +1, an increase, so oxidised.
cards.why: This reaction makes household bleach (sodium chlorate(I)).

cards.q: Chlorine reacts with water: \(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + H_{2}O \rightleftharpoons HCl + HClO}\). Give the oxidation numbers of chlorine and explain why this is disproportionation.
cards.a: Cl is 0 in Cl₂, −1 in HCl and +1 in HClO: the same element is both reduced and oxidised.
cards.why: This is the reaction used when water supplies are chlorinated.

cards.q: Copper(I) ions in aqueous solution disproportionate. Write the equation and give the oxidation number changes.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{2Cu^{+}(aq) \rightarrow Cu(s) + Cu^{2+}(aq)}\)
steps: The other loses an electron: +1 \(\rightarrow\) +2, oxidised.
cards.why: A d-block example: a pink-brown copper solid and a blue solution form.

cards.q: What is a half-equation?
cards.a: An equation for either the oxidation or the reduction part of a redox reaction alone, with electrons shown.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^{-}}\) (oxidation); \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow Cu}\) (reduction).

cards.q: List the steps for balancing a half-equation for a reaction in acidic solution.
cards.a:
1. Balance the atoms of the element changing oxidation number.
2. Balance O by adding \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\).
3. Balance H by adding \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\).
4. Balance charge by adding electrons.
cards.why: Check: the number of electrons equals the total change in oxidation number.

cards.q: Write the half-equation for the reduction of manganate(VII) ions, \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\), to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) in acid.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}(aq) + 8H^{+}(aq) + 5e^{-} \rightarrow Mn^{2+}(aq) + 4H_{2}O(l)}\)
cards.why: Mn goes from +7 to +2: five electrons. Charge: −1 + 8 − 5 = +2 on both sides.

cards.q: Write the half-equation for the reduction of dichromate(VI) ions to chromium(III) ions in acid.
cards.why: Two Cr each go from +6 to +3: six electrons. Charge: −2 + 14 − 6 = +6 on both sides.

cards.q: Write the half-equation for the oxidation of hydrogen peroxide to oxygen.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}(aq) \rightarrow O_{2}(g) + 2H^{+}(aq) + 2e^{-}}\)
cards.why: Each O goes from −1 to 0, two O atoms: two electrons.

cards.q: Write the half-equation for the oxidation of ethanedioate ions, \(\mathrm{C_{2}O_{4}^{2-}}\), to carbon dioxide.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{2}O_{4}^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow 2CO_{2}(g) + 2e^{-}}\)
cards.why: Two C atoms each go from +3 to +4: two electrons.

cards.q: Write the half-equations for the reaction between iodine and thiosulfate ions.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{I_{2}(aq) + 2e^{-} \rightarrow 2I^{-}(aq)}\)
\(\mathrm{2S_{2}O_{3}^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow S_{4}O_{6}^{2-}(aq) + 2e^{-}}\)
cards.why: Iodine is reduced; thiosulfate is oxidised to tetrathionate (S from +2 to +2.5, four S atoms: two electrons).

cards.q: How are two half-equations combined to give an overall redox equation?
cards.a: Multiply one or both so the number of electrons lost equals the number gained, add them together, then cancel the electrons and any species on both sides.
cards.why: Electrons must never appear in the overall equation.

cards.q: Combine the half-equations to give the overall equation for the reaction of acidified manganate(VII) ions with iron(II) ions.
cards.why: Multiply \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+} + e^{-}}\) by 5 to match the five electrons gained by \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\). Mole ratio \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-} : Fe^{2+} = 1 : 5}\).

cards.q: Write the overall equation for the reaction of acidified dichromate(VI) ions with iron(II) ions.
cards.why: Six \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) supply the six electrons. Charge check: \(-2 + 14 + 12 = +24\); \(+6 + 18 = +24\).

cards.q: Write the overall equation for the reaction of acidified manganate(VII) ions with ethanedioate ions.
cards.why: Ten electrons: double the manganate half-equation and multiply the ethanedioate one by 5. Mole ratio \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-} : C_{2}O_{4}^{2-} = 2 : 5}\).

cards.q: Write the overall equation for the reaction of acidified manganate(VII) ions with hydrogen peroxide.
cards.why: Adding the half-equations gives \(\mathrm{16H^{+}}\) on the left and \(\mathrm{10H^{+}}\) on the right; cancel to leave \(\mathrm{6H^{+}}\). Ratio \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-} : H_{2}O_{2} = 2 : 5}\).

cards.q: Write the overall ionic equation for the reaction between iodine and thiosulfate ions.
cards.why: Mole ratio \(\mathrm{I_{2} : S_{2}O_{3}^{2-} = 1 : 2}\), the key ratio in every iodine–thiosulfate titration.

cards.q: Write half-equations and the overall ionic equation for chlorine displacing bromine from bromide ions.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow 2Cl^{-}}\)
\(\mathrm{2Br^{-} \rightarrow Br_{2} + 2e^{-}}\)
Overall: \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}(aq) + 2Br^{-}(aq) \rightarrow 2Cl^{-}(aq) + Br_{2}(aq)}\)
cards.why: The colourless solution turns orange/yellow as bromine forms.

cards.q: In a titration with potassium manganate(VII), why is no indicator needed and what is the end point?
cards.a: \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\) is deep purple and is reduced to almost colourless \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), so it acts as its own indicator. The end point is the first permanent pale pink colour.
cards.why: The pink appears when there is a slight excess of manganate(VII) that has nothing left to react with.

cards.q: Explain why manganate(VII) titrations are acidified with dilute sulfuric acid rather than hydrochloric acid, and why the acid must be in excess.
cards.a: Sulfuric acid supplies the H⁺ without reacting with manganate(VII).
marks: \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) ions are needed for the reduction of \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\) to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\).
Hydrochloric acid would be oxidised by manganate(VII) to chlorine.
Extra manganate(VII) would then be used, so the titre would be too large.
Too little acid gives brown \(\mathrm{MnO_{2}}\) instead of \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), so the 1 : 5 ratio no longer applies.

cards.q: In an iodine–thiosulfate titration, when is starch added and what is the end point?
cards.a: Add starch near the end point, when the iodine colour has faded to pale yellow (straw). The end point is when the blue-black colour disappears, leaving a colourless solution.
cards.why: If starch is added too early, a lot of iodine binds to it and is released only slowly, so the end point is hard to see.

cards.q: How can iodine–thiosulfate titration be used to find the amount of an oxidising agent?
cards.a: Add the oxidising agent to an excess of potassium iodide. It oxidises iodide ions to iodine; the iodine released is then titrated with standard sodium thiosulfate.
cards.why: Link the amounts through the equations: for example \(\mathrm{2Cu^{2+} + 4I^{-} \rightarrow 2CuI + I_{2}}\), then \(\mathrm{I_{2} + 2S_{2}O_{3}^{2-}}\), so \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+} : S_{2}O_{3}^{2-} = 1 : 1}\).

cards.q: 25.0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of iron(II) solution reacts with 21.60 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of 0.0200 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) acidified potassium manganate(VII). Calculate the concentration of iron(II) ions.
cards.a: 0.0864 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
cards.why: A structured calculation: moles of titrant → ratio → moles of analyte → concentration.

cards.q: An iron tablet is dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid and made up to 250 \(\text{cm}^{3}\). 25.0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) portions need a mean of 12.40 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of 0.00200 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) \(\mathrm{KMnO_{4}}\). Calculate the mass of iron, in mg, in the tablet. (\(A_{\text{r}}\) Fe \(= 55.8\))
cards.a: 69.2 mg
cards.why: Remember the scale-up: only a tenth of the solution was titrated.

cards.q: 25.0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of ethanedioic acid solution is warmed and titrated with 0.0200 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) acidified \(\mathrm{KMnO_{4}}\); the mean titre is 24.00 \(\text{cm}^{3}\). Calculate the concentration of the ethanedioic acid.
cards.a: 0.0480 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
cards.why: Get the ratio from the balanced overall equation, not from the electrons alone.

cards.q: A sample of hair bleach is diluted. 25.0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of the diluted solution needs 20.00 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of 0.0200 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) acidified \(\mathrm{KMnO_{4}}\). Calculate the concentration of hydrogen peroxide in the diluted solution.
cards.a: 0.0400 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
cards.why: To find the concentration in the original bleach, multiply by the dilution factor.

cards.q: 25.0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of iodine solution needs 18.60 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of 0.100 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) sodium thiosulfate. Calculate the concentration of the iodine solution.
cards.a: 0.0372 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
cards.why: Halve the moles of thiosulfate to get moles of iodine.

cards.q: 10.0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of diluted bleach is added to excess acidified KI: \(\mathrm{ClO^{-} + 2I^{-} + 2H^{+} \rightarrow Cl^{-} + I_{2} + H_{2}O}\). The iodine needs 15.60 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of 0.0500 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) \(\mathrm{Na_{2}S_{2}O_{3}}\). Find the concentration of \(\mathrm{ClO^{-}}\).
cards.a: 0.0390 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
cards.why: Chain the ratios: \(\mathrm{ClO^{-} : I_{2} : S_{2}O_{3}^{2-} = 1 : 1 : 2}\).

cards.q: 0.200 g of brass is dissolved and neutralised, then excess KI is added. The iodine released needs 21.80 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of 0.100 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) sodium thiosulfate. Calculate the percentage by mass of copper in the brass. (\(A_{\text{r}}\) Cu \(= 63.5\))
cards.a: 69.2%
cards.why: A non-structured calculation: build the mole ratio yourself from the two equations.

cards.q: Why is the burette reading taken from the top of the meniscus in a potassium manganate(VII) titration?
cards.a: The solution is so deeply coloured that the bottom of the meniscus cannot be seen clearly.
cards.why: As long as the same point is read each time, the titre (a difference) is still accurate.

cards.q: True or false: oxygen always has an oxidation number of −2 in its compounds.
cards.a: False. It is −1 in peroxides such as \(\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}\) and +2 in \(\mathrm{OF_{2}}\).
cards.why: Check whether the compound is a peroxide before applying the usual value.

cards.q: True or false: in a half-equation, electrons are added to balance the number of atoms.
cards.a: False. Electrons balance the charge. Atoms are balanced with H₂O and H⁺.
cards.why: The number of electrons should equal the total change in oxidation number.

cards.q: True or false: \(\mathrm{Zn + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + Cu}\) is a disproportionation because one species is oxidised and another is reduced.
cards.a: False. It is redox, but not disproportionation.
cards.why: Disproportionation needs the same element in one species to be both oxidised and reduced; here two different elements change.
